questions.prompt: A PowerShell -EncodedCommand value, once Base64-decoded, produces garbled text with null bytes between characters. What's the most likely explanation?
options: The command is corrupted and unrecoverable
The text is UTF-16LE encoded, and needs a Unicode decode step after the Base64 decode
The command was encrypted, not encoded
questions.explanation: PowerShell's -EncodedCommand encodes UTF-16LE text as Base64. Skipping the UTF-16LE decode step after Base64-decoding is the most common mistake, and produces exactly this null-byte-between-characters pattern.

questions.prompt: What is the most likely reason a decoded -EncodedCommand payload is still unreadable binary data rather than plain text?
options: The decode was done incorrectly and should be retried the same way
A compression layer (like GzipStream or DeflateStream) was applied before Base64 encoding, and needs its own decompression step
The command uses a newer PowerShell version
Encoded commands longer than 100 characters are automatically corrupted
questions.explanation: Attackers commonly compress a payload before Base64-encoding it as a second obfuscation layer, which means the standard Base64/UTF-16LE decode alone still leaves compressed binary data requiring a matching decompression step.

questions.prompt: Why might Script Block Logging make manual decoding of an -EncodedCommand unnecessary in many cases?
options: Script Block Logging blocks encoded commands from running at all
Event ID 4104 already captures the script after PowerShell's parser has processed and reconstructed it
Encoded commands are illegal and always get flagged automatically
Manual decoding is never necessary for any PowerShell evidence
questions.explanation: As covered in the previous lesson, Script Block Logging records the post-parse script text -- so when 4104 is available, the deobfuscated content is often already sitting in the log.

questions.prompt: Why is the process command-line field (Event ID 4688 or Sysmon Event ID 1) sometimes an unreliable source for a full -EncodedCommand value?
options: Command lines are never logged for PowerShell processes
Very long command lines can be truncated depending on log configuration and collection method
Encoded commands are stored in a separate, encrypted log
4688 only logs the process name, never any arguments
questions.explanation: Long command lines -- which encoded payloads often are -- can be truncated in process-creation logs depending on configuration, silently cutting off part of the encoded blob. Script Block Logging avoids this limitation.
